name: AI for Real Estate Agents
objectives: Given verified facts from records, the seller and your own visit, write a listing description with AI help and check every fact line by line, removing anything you cannot verify

Given a listing or ad written with AI, identify and rewrite language that shows a preference about people instead of describing the property, so every line describes only the property and its features

Given a checked listing, create a social post and a marketing email that follow licensee advertising and email rules, with license and brokerage details as required, a postal address and an unsubscribe option
Given your rough notes from the week, write a seller or buyer update with AI using placeholders for private details, with no client private information in the AI tool
Given a new lead who agreed to hear from you, plan a 30-day follow-up with four helpful messages and a tracked next date, with any program links checked on official pages
Given market numbers you pulled from your MLS, create a plain-words market summary and an open-house checklist, with no invented numbers and the source and date added

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Writing listing descriptions from your facts
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write an accurate, appealing listing description from verified property facts.
This lesson builds toward: Given verified facts from records, the seller and your own visit, you will write a listing description with AI help and check every fact line by line, removing anything you cannot verify.
A listing description sells the home's features: layout, updates, light, outdoor space, location features like nearby parks or transit. AI writes fast, but it only knows what you tell it.
Give it verified facts only: "3 bed, 2 bath, 1,450 sq ft per county records, built 1962, kitchen remodeled 2021, new roof 2023, fenced backyard with lemon tree, 0.3 miles to light rail." Ask for a 120-word description in a warm, professional tone, and a short version for social media.
Then check every fact: square footage source, year of updates, school names, distances. AI may add things that are not there ("granite counters", "ocean view"). Misstatements in a listing can lead to complaints and legal trouble.
Step by step:
- Gather verified facts from records, the seller and your own visit.
- Ask AI for a long and a short description.
- Check every fact line by line.
- Remove anything you cannot verify.
Words to know:
- Listing description: the written text that describes a property for sale or rent.
- MLS: Multiple Listing Service: the database agents use to share listings.
- Verified fact: something you have confirmed from records, the seller or your own visit.
Try it now: Pick a property you know (or a sample). Write ten verified facts, ask AI for a 120-word description, and check every line, deleting anything not in your facts.
You can now write a listing description from verified facts and catch AI's made-up details.

check.q: What does AI know about a home when it writes a listing?
options: What the seller told your office
check.why: AI only knows what you give it, so you give it verified facts only.

check.q: AI's listing says "granite counters" but you did not see them on your visit. What do you do?
options: Remove it unless you can verify it
Ask AI if it is sure
check.why: You check every fact and remove anything you cannot verify.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Fair housing language: what AI must not write
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Spot and fix listing language that shows a preference based on a protected class.
This lesson builds toward: Given a listing or ad written with AI, you will identify and rewrite language that shows a preference about people instead of describing the property, so every line describes only the property and its features.
The federal Fair Housing Act prohibits housing discrimination because of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status and disability. HUD's rule at 24 CFR 100.75 bans ads, statements and notices that show a preference, limitation or discrimination based on these, including through words, photos or where you choose to advertise. Many states, including California, protect more groups; check your state.
Describe the property, not the people you want to live there. Risky phrases: "perfect for young professionals", "ideal for a couple", "no kids", "great Christian neighborhood", "bachelor pad", "walking distance to [a house of worship] for families of that faith", "able-bodied". Better: "three bedrooms", "quiet street", "0.3 miles to transit", "single-level layout".
AI can copy biased patterns from what it learned. Always read its output for fair housing problems, and ask it: "Rewrite to describe only the property and its features." When unsure, ask your broker or a fair housing resource.
Step by step:
- Read every line asking: does this describe the property or the people?
- Remove words about who should live there.
- Replace with property features.
- Check photos and ad placement too.
- Ask your broker when unsure.
Words to know:
- Fair Housing Act: the federal law that bans housing discrimination based on protected classes.
- Protected class: a group the law protects from discrimination, such as race or familial status.
- Familial status: having children under 18 in the household, or being pregnant.
- HUD: the US Department of Housing and Urban Development.
Official sources:
- HUD: Fair Housing Act overview
- 24 CFR 100.75: Discriminatory advertisements, statements and notices
Try it now: Ask AI for a listing description of a family-sized home. Mark every phrase that describes people instead of the property, then rewrite them as features.
You can now spot and fix fair housing problems in listing language, including AI-written text.

options: The kind of people who should buy
Who will fit in on the street
check.why: Describe the property, not the people you want to live there.

check.q: AI writes "ideal for a couple." What do you do?
options: Replace it with property features, such as "two bedrooms, quiet street"
check.why: "Ideal for a couple" is a risky phrase about people; describe the property instead.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Marketing your listings and yourself, by the rules
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Create social posts and emails for a listing that follow advertising and email rules.
This lesson builds toward: Given a checked listing, you will create a social post and a marketing email that follow licensee advertising and email rules, with license and brokerage details as required, a postal address and an unsubscribe option.
AI can turn your checked listing into posts, an email to your sphere, flyer text and a short video script. Use the same verified facts and the same fair housing check for every piece.
Your state regulator and your broker have advertising rules for licensees, often including showing your license number and brokerage name. In California, that regulator is the Department of Real Estate (DRE); check your own state's rules and your brokerage policy.
Marketing emails must follow CAN-SPAM: honest sender and subject, identify it as an ad, include a postal address and an unsubscribe option, and honor opt-outs within 10 business days.
Step by step:
- Turn the checked listing into a post, an email and a flyer with AI.
- Run the fair housing check on each.
- Add license and brokerage details as your state and broker require.
- Add a postal address and unsubscribe to marketing emails.
Words to know:
- Sphere: the people you know who might buy, sell or refer: past clients, friends, family.
- Licensee: a person holding a real estate license.
Official sources:
- California Department of Real Estate (example state regulator)
- FTC: CAN-SPAM Act, A Compliance Guide for Business
Try it now: Turn your checked listing into a social post and a short email. Run the fair housing check, and add the license and brokerage details your state and broker require.
You can now market a listing across channels while following fair housing, licensee and email rules.

check.q: Which email rule covers marketing emails in this lesson?
check.why: Marketing emails must follow CAN-SPAM, including a postal address and an unsubscribe option.

check.q: You turn your listing into a social post with AI. What else do you do before posting?
options: Post it right away; the listing was already checked
Run the fair housing check and add license and brokerage details as required
Add a stock photo of a different home
check.why: Every piece gets the same fair housing check and the details your state and broker require.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Clients, leads and market data

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Client updates without sharing private information
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn your notes into clear seller and buyer updates using placeholders.
This lesson builds toward: Given your rough notes from the week, you will write a seller or buyer update with AI using placeholders for private details, with no client private information in the AI tool.
Clients want to hear from you often. A weekly seller update covers showings, feedback, online views and next steps. A buyer update covers new matches, scheduled showings and what is happening in their price range.
Use AI to turn rough notes into a clear update, with placeholders: "Turn these notes into a friendly weekly update for [seller name]: 6 showings, 2 second showings, feedback says kitchen is great but backyard needs cleanup, 1,200 online views. Suggest one next step."
Never put client private details into AI tools: full names with addresses, financial information, pre-approval amounts, Social Security numbers, offer terms or negotiation strategy. Fill those in yourself in your email or CRM. Follow your brokerage's rules on AI tools.
Step by step:
- Write rough notes after the week.
- Replace names and private details with placeholders.
- Ask AI for a clear update with a next step.
- Fill in the real details yourself and send.
Words to know:
- CRM: customer relationship management: software for tracking clients and leads.
- Placeholder: a blank like [seller name] used instead of real private details.
Try it now: Write rough notes for a sample seller's week. Use placeholders, ask AI for a weekly update with a next step, and check it has no private details.
You can now send clear client updates made with AI while keeping client information private.

check.q: What does a weekly seller update cover?
options: Showings, feedback, online views and next steps
check.why: A seller update covers showings, feedback, views and next steps.

check.q: Your notes include the buyer's full name and offer terms. What do you do before pasting them into AI?
options: Replace private details with placeholders and fill them in yourself later
check.why: Client private details stay out of AI tools; you fill them in yourself.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: A follow-up plan for leads
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a 30-day follow-up plan with four messages for new leads.
This lesson builds toward: Given a new lead who agreed to hear from you, you will plan a 30-day follow-up with four helpful messages and a tracked next date, with any program links checked on official pages.
Most leads are not ready today. A steady, helpful follow-up plan keeps you in mind. Example 30-day plan: day 1 thank-you and one question; day 7 useful tip (first-time buyer programs to look into); day 14 market snapshot for their area; day 30 check-in.
Ask AI to write each message in your voice with [first name] and [area] blanks. Keep them helpful, not pushy. Give links only to official program pages you have checked.
Track leads in your CRM or a spreadsheet: name, source, date, stage, next follow-up date. Only email or text people who agreed to hear from you, and follow email and texting rules.
Step by step:
- Plan four touches over 30 days.
- Ask AI to draft each with blanks.
- Make them helpful and check any program details on official pages.
- Track each lead's next follow-up date.
- Contact only people who agreed.
Words to know:
- Lead: a person who might buy, sell or rent but has not signed with you.
- Touch: one contact with a lead: a call, text or email.
Try it now: Ask AI to draft your four-message, 30-day follow-up plan. Edit each into your voice and set up a lead tracking sheet with a next-follow-up column.
You can now run a consistent, helpful follow-up plan for new leads.

check.q: In the example plan, what is the day-14 message?
options: A market snapshot for their area
check.why: The plan is day 1 thank-you, day 7 tip, day 14 market snapshot, day 30 check-in.

check.q: You met someone at a party who never agreed to hear from you. Should you add them to your text plan?
options: Yes, anyone you meet is a lead
No, only contact people who agreed to hear from you
Yes, if the messages are short
check.why: Only email or text people who agreed, and follow email and texting rules.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Market summaries and showing prep
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn market numbers you pulled into a clear client summary, and prep an open house.
This lesson builds toward: Given market numbers you pulled from your MLS, you will create a plain-words market summary and an open-house checklist, with no invented numbers and the source and date added.
Clients ask, "What is the market doing?" Pull the numbers yourself from your MLS or another reliable source: median price, days on market, number of active listings, sale-to-list price ratio, for the last few months.
Paste the numbers (no client data) into AI and ask: "Explain these market numbers for a first-time buyer in plain words, in 150 words. Do not add numbers I did not give you." Check that it did not invent statistics, and add your source and date. AI does not have reliable live market data; you do.
For showings and open houses, ask AI for a checklist: before (lights, temperature, flyers, sign-in), during (safety, greeting, notes), after (follow-up within 24 hours). Add your brokerage's safety practices.
Step by step:
- Pull current numbers from your MLS or a reliable source.
- Ask AI to explain them in plain words without adding numbers.
- Check every number and add source and date.
- Ask AI for an open-house checklist and add safety steps.
Words to know:
- Median price: the middle price: half of homes sold for more, half for less.
- Days on market: how long homes take to sell.
- Sale-to-list ratio: sale price divided by list price, shown as a percent.
Try it now: Final task: build your agent AI kit: a checked listing description, seller and buyer update templates, the 30-day follow-up plan, a market summary from numbers you pulled, and an open-house checklist.
You can now explain market numbers clearly and prepare showings with AI help, using your own data.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Accurate listing The listing has a fact that was not verified, such as a feature the home does not have. Every fact is checked line by line against records, the seller or your visit. Notes the source of key facts such as square footage. Fair housing language A line describes who should live there instead of the property. Every line describes only the property and its features. Also checks photos and ad placement and can explain each fix. Private client updates A client name with address, financial detail or offer terms went into the AI tool. Seller and buyer update templates use placeholders, with a clear next step. Placeholders are filled in only in the agent's own email or CRM. Lead follow-up plan Fewer than four messages, or messages are pushy or unchecked. Four helpful messages over 30 days with blanks and a tracked next date. Program links are checked on official pages and noted. Market summary and open house The summary has a number not pulled from your source. Plain-words summary from your own numbers with source and date, plus an open-house checklist. The checklist includes brokerage safety steps and follow-up within 24 hours. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does sale-to-list price ratio compare?
options: What homes sold for to what they were listed for
check.why: It compares the sale price with the list price.

check.q: AI's market summary includes a number you did not give it. What do you do?
options: Keep it; AI has live data
Remove it and check every number against your source
check.why: AI does not have reliable live market data, so you remove invented numbers and add your source and date.
